Jeremiah's Incarceration by Pashur, the Principal Officer of the Temple, for Prophesying within Its Precincts; His Renewed Predictions against the City, &c., ON His Liberation.</title> <div sID="gen17854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10023"/><hi type="bold">1. son--</hi>descendant.<div eID="gen17854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Immer--</hi>one of the original "governors of the sanctuary and of the house of God," twenty-four in all, that is, sixteen of the sons of Eleazar and eight of the sons of Ithamar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.14">1Ch 24:14</reference>). This Pashur is distinct from Pashur, son of Melchiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>). The "captains" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.4">Lu 22:4</reference>) seem to have been over the twenty-four guards of the temple, and had only the right of apprehending any who were guilty of delinquency within it; but the Sanhedrim had the judicial power over such delinquents [Grotius] (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.8">Jr 26:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.16">10, 16</reference>). <div eID="gen17855" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 20 Jr 20:1-18 . This Pashur is distinct from Pashur, son of Melchiah ( Jr 21:1 ). The "captains" ( Lu 22:4 ) seem to have been over the twenty-four guards of the temple, and had only the right of apprehending any who were guilty of delinquency within it; but the Sanhedrim had the judicial power over such delinquents [Grotius] ( Jr 26:8 , 10, 16 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10026"/><div sID="gen17861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10026"/><hi type="bold">4. terror ... to all thy friends--</hi>who have believed thy false promises (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.6">Jr 20:6</reference>). The sense must be in order to accord with "fear round about" (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.3">Jr 20:3</reference>). I will bring terror on thee and on all thy friends, that terror arising from thyself, namely, thy false prophecies. Thou and thy prophecies will be seen, to the dismay both of thee and thy dupes, to have caused their ruin and thine. Maurer's translation is therefore not needed, "I will give up thee and all thy friends to terror." <div eID="gen17861" type="x-p"/>

Jeremiah's complaint, not unlike that of Job, breathing somewhat of human infirmity in consequence of his imprisonment. Thou didst promise never to give me up to the will of mine enemies, and yet Thou hast done so. But Jeremiah misunderstood God's promise, which was not that he should have nothing to suffer, but that God would deliver him out of sufferings (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.19">Jr 1:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceived--</hi>Others translate as Margin, "Thou hast enticed" or "persuaded me," namely, to undertake the prophetic office, "and I was persuaded," that is, suffered myself to be persuaded to undertake what I find too hard for me. So the Hebrew word is used in a good sense (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.27">Ge 9:27</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.15">Pr 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.14">Ho 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen17866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stronger than I--</hi>Thou whose strength I could not resist hast laid this burden on me, and hast prevailed (hast made me prophesy, in spite of my reluctance) (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.5-Jer.1.7">Jr 1:5-7</reference>); yet, when I exercise my office, I am treated with derision (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.14">La 3:14</reference>). <div eID="gen17867" type="x-p"/>

The "defaming" or detraction of the enemy on every side (see <reference osisRef="Ps.31.13">Psa 31:13</reference>) tempted him to think of prophesying no more.<div eID="gen17872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Report ... we will report--</hi>The words of his adversaries one to the other; give any information against him (true or false) which will give color for accusing him; and "we will report it," namely, to the Sanhedrim, in order to crush him.<div eID="gen17873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">familiars--</hi>literally, "men of my peace"; those who pretended to be on peaceable terms with me (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>). Jeremiah is a type of Messiah, referred to in that Psalm. (See <reference osisRef="Jer.38.22">Jr 38:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.19">Job 19:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.13">Psa 55:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.53">Lu 11:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.54">54</reference>).<div eID="gen17874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watched for my halting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Psa 35:15</reference>, Margin, "halting"; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.10">71:10</reference>, Margin). The Hebrew means properly "side," then "halting," as the halt bend on one side. enticed-- to commit some sin.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10036"/><div sID="gen17882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10036"/>14-18. The contrast between the spirit of this passage and the preceding thanksgiving is to be explained thus: to show how great was the deliverance (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.13">Jr 20:13</reference>), he subjoins a picture of what his wounded spirit had been previous to his deliverance; I had said in the time of my imprisonment, "Cursed be the day"; my feeling was that of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.3.3">Job 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.10.11">10, 11</reference>, whose words Jeremiah therefore copies). Though Jeremiah's zeal had been stirred up, not so much for self as for God's honor trampled on by the rejection of the prophet's words, yet it was intemperate when he made his birth a subject for cursing, which was really a ground for thanksgiving. <div eID="gen17882" type="x-p"/>

The contrast between the spirit of this passage and the preceding thanksgiving is to be explained thus: to show how great was the deliverance ( Jr 20:13 ), he subjoins a picture of what his wounded spirit had been previous to his deliverance; I had said in the time of my imprisonment, "Cursed be the day"; my feeling was that of Job ( Job 3:3 , 10, 11 , whose words Jeremiah therefore copies). Though Jeremiah's zeal had been stirred up, not so much for self as for God's honor trampled on by the rejection of the prophet's words, yet it was intemperate when he made his birth a subject for cursing, which was really a ground for thanksgiving.
